domains.name: Exams & Timed Performance
domains.summary: This domain covers university examinations and timed performance: understanding exam formats, analysing exam questions, planning revision, writing under time pressure, approaching objective-format questions, open-book and take-home exams, oral examinations and managing test anxiety. It draws on cognitive research on retrieval and spacing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Roediger & Karpicke, 2006), research on planning under time pressure (Ellis & Yuan, 2004), writing assessment (Weigle, 2002) and test anxiety (Putwain, 2008; Horwitz et al., 1986). Emphasis is on matching preparation and in-exam behaviour to the demands of each format rather than on generic exam tips.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how different university exams work, how to read exam questions precisely, how to revise so that you remember, how to write and speak well under time pressure, and how to manage exam nerves.

stageEmphasis.foundation: First experience of university-style exams in subject modules: formats, question analysis, revision planning and timed writing, often alongside content learning in English.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Timed writing and oral assessment as part of progression, with attention to question analysis and managing anxiety in high-stakes conditions.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Support before exam seasons: revision planning, exam essays and short answers, objective-format papers and open-book or take-home exams.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid preparation for unfamiliar formats (seen papers, take-home exams, case-based exams) within a compressed year.

domains.name: Feedback & Assessment Literacy
domains.summary: This domain covers how learners come to understand university assessment and use feedback: assessment purposes and rules, grading systems, marking criteria, feedback literacy, acting on feedback, using written corrective feedback, seeking feedback and self- and peer-assessment. It draws on Sadler's (1989) argument that learners must come to share the assessor's concept of quality, on feedback as a support for self-regulation (Nicol & Macfarlane-Dick, 2006; Hattie & Timperley, 2007) and on student feedback literacy (Carless & Boud, 2018). On written corrective feedback, the contested evidence (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999; Bitchener & Ferris, 2012; Kang & Han, 2015) should be presented honestly.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how university assessment works, what marking criteria and grades really mean, and how to ask for, understand and act on feedback so that each assignment improves the next.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explicit introduction to formative and summative assessment, local grading conventions and rubrics, often the learner's first encounter with criterion-referenced coursework.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Intensive use of criteria, exemplars, correction codes and draft-feedback cycles leading to the progression assessment.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Interpreting disciplinary criteria and feedback on early assignments, and building feed-forward habits across modules.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid calibration to master's-level standards, where marks are often lower than learners expect and feedback windows are short.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Seeking and negotiating feedback from supervisors, peers and reviewers, and developing the evaluative judgement needed to review one's own and others' research writing.

domains.name: Self-Regulated Learning
domains.summary: This domain covers the knowledge and strategies that let learners direct their own academic and language development: metacognitive knowledge, the self-regulation cycle, autonomy, motivation, goal setting, time management, study techniques, language learning strategies, reflective logs, support services, wellbeing and learning content through English. It is anchored in self-regulated learning research (Zimmerman, 2002; Flavell, 1979), autonomy research (Holec, 1981; Benson, 2011) and cognitive research on durable learning (Dunlosky et al., 2013). These topics are best taught through learners' real tasks and evidence (feedback, self-test results, time logs), not as detached 'study skills'.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn how to plan, monitor and evaluate your own learning, choose study methods that actually work, manage your time and wellbeing, and keep developing your English after your course ends.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Explicit, scaffolded introduction to independent study, time management and evidence-informed study techniques, linked to the shift from school to university-style learning.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Compressed work on goal setting, reflective logs and study techniques tied to weekly tasks and the progression decision, with an eye to continued development during the degree.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Embedded support at transition points (first assessments, first exam season), focusing on time management, study techniques and use of support services.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid orientation to a dense one-year programme: workload planning, independent study expectations and strategies for learning disciplinary content and language together.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Self-regulation across long, loosely structured projects: goal setting, time management, wellbeing and use of researcher development and supervisory support.

domains.name: Proficiency Tests & Progression
domains.summary: This domain helps learners understand the language assessments that control access to and progression through university study: the purposes of different assessments, CEFR levels and entry requirements, the formats and constructs of academic proficiency tests, the differences between test tasks and university tasks, strategies for integrated test tasks, and pre-sessional progression assessment. It draws on language assessment theory (Bachman & Palmer, 2010; Weigle, 2002), the CEFR (Council of Europe, 2001, 2020; North, 2014) and research on test washback and on the gap between test and university writing (Green, 2007; Moore & Morton, 2005). Test formats, score requirements and visa rules change, so content is framed at the level of task types and constructs, and learners are directed to current official sources.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn what language tests and progression assessments are for, what their scores do and do not tell you, how test tasks differ from university work, and how to prepare without letting the test narrow your learning.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Understanding entry and progression requirements and test formats, while building the broader academic literacy that tests only partly measure.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional: Central: understanding the progression assessment, how it relates to entry requirements and proficiency tests, and moving from test-oriented habits to university-oriented ones.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Addressing the transition from test preparation to disciplinary writing, especially where first-year students carry test templates into coursework.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Rapid recalibration for master's students who entered directly with a test score and must adjust from test tasks to source-based disciplinary writing.

topics.name: University exam formats
topics.description: Understand the main formats of university examination (unseen and seen written papers, open-book and take-home exams, multiple-choice and short-answer tests, problem-based papers, oral and practical examinations such as OSCEs in health programmes, and computer-based or online variants) and what kind of knowledge and performance each rewards, so that preparation and in-exam behaviour match the format.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the format of each exam on their programme using handbooks and past papers
Explains how preparation differs for seen, unseen, open-book and objective-format exams
Identifies what each format typically rewards (recall, application, synthesis or performance)
Locates and uses past papers, exam regulations and information on permitted materials
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three brief exam descriptions (a seen-question paper, a 24-hour open-book paper, a multiple-choice test across the whole syllabus) and ask how preparation should differ for each. Look for format-specific preparation (planning answers to seen questions, organising and indexing materials for open-book, retrieval practice across the syllabus for multiple choice) rather than 'revise everything'.

topics.name: Analysing exam questions
topics.description: Analyse an exam question quickly and accurately, identifying the command word or words, topic, focus and limiting words, implicit sub-questions and the expected answer type, and allocate time across questions in proportion to marks.
masteryEvidence: Marks the command, topic, focus and limiting words in a question and paraphrases what it requires
Identifies multi-part questions and implicit sub-questions, such as the judgement of degree required by 'to what extent'
Distinguishes questions inviting description from those requiring evaluation or argument
Allocates time per question in proportion to marks, including time for planning and checking
Recognises when a question that superficially matches a revised topic actually asks for something different
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three exam questions on the same topic with different command words and limiting phrases (for example, 'Outline…', 'Critically evaluate… with reference to…', 'To what extent… since 2010?'). Ask the learner what a good answer to each would do. Look for distinctions in the shape of the answer and attention to limiting words; treating all three as 'write about the topic' indicates a gap.

topics.name: Planning revision
topics.description: Plan revision as a spaced, active schedule that begins weeks before the exam period: mapping the syllabus and past-paper demands, distributing sessions across topics, building sessions around retrieval and timed practice, and adjusting the plan according to self-test results.
masteryEvidence: Produces a revision timetable that starts several weeks before exams and revisits each topic more than once
Builds sessions around retrieval (self-testing, past questions, blank-page recall) rather than rereading
Uses self-test results to move time towards weaker topics
Includes timed practice under exam-like conditions for written papers
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show their revision plan for an upcoming exam. Check the start date, spacing and revisiting of topics, the types of activity and the use of past papers; a plan that consists of reading notes once per topic in the final week indicates a gap.

topics.name: Timed writing
topics.description: Produce coherent, relevant written answers under time pressure: planning rapidly (a brief outline and a position), allocating time between planning, writing and checking, writing fluently without sources to hand, and checking for one's own most frequent errors. Applies to exam essays, short-answer papers and timed tasks in language tests and progression assessments.
masteryEvidence: Spends a small, planned share of the available time on a brief outline with a position before writing
Produces an answer whose opening addresses the question directly and whose paragraphs each advance the answer
Completes all required answers within the time, prioritising by marks
Reserves time to check for their own known high-frequency errors
Adapts memorised content to the specific question rather than reproducing it wholesale
topics.assessmentPrompt: Set an unseen question with a fixed time limit and observe the first few minutes. Then examine the script: is there a visible plan, does the introduction answer the question, does each paragraph advance a point, and was the final section completed? Compare the plan with the script to see whether planning was used or abandoned.

topics.name: Objective question strategies
topics.description: Approach multiple-choice, true/false, matching and short-item questions strategically: reading stems precisely (including negatives and qualifiers), predicting an answer before reading the options, eliminating distractors for stated reasons, managing time and flagged items, and applying the paper's rules on guessing and negative marking.
masteryEvidence: Identifies negatives, absolutes and qualifiers in a stem or option and explains how they change the answer
Generates an answer from knowledge before viewing the options when the stem allows
Eliminates options for specific reasons and returns to flagged items
Applies the stated scoring rules, such as negative marking, when deciding whether to answer uncertain items
Distinguishes items testing recall from those testing application and adjusts reading time accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five multiple-choice items from the learner's subject (or based on a general academic text), including one 'NOT' item, one with an absolute qualifier and one application item. Ask the learner to think aloud while answering. Look for close reading of qualifiers, reasoned elimination and correct handling of the negative; choosing options because their wording looks familiar indicates surface processing.

topics.name: Open-book and take-home exams
topics.description: Prepare for and complete open-book and take-home exams, recognising that they assess application, analysis and synthesis rather than recall: organising and indexing permitted materials in advance, managing extended time windows, and observing paper-specific rules on collaboration, sources, citation and AI use.
masteryEvidence: Prepares an organised, indexed set of notes and sources that can be navigated quickly
Answers by applying and synthesising material rather than reproducing notes or lecture slides
Cites sources in take-home answers to the standard the paper requires
States the rules on collaboration, permitted resources and AI use for a given paper and plans to work within them
Plans time across a take-home window, including breaks and a final check
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a take-home question and the learner's own notes on the topic. Ask them to sketch an answer plan in a short, fixed time and to state what they may and may not do (consult peers, use AI tools, reuse lecture slides). Look for application rather than reproduction of notes, an accurate statement of the rules and planned citation.

topics.name: Oral examinations
topics.description: Prepare for and perform in oral assessments such as questioning on submitted work, individual oral examinations, interactive orals and the speaking components of language assessments: anticipating question types, structuring spoken answers, asking for clarification or repetition, gaining thinking time appropriately and recovering from breakdowns.
masteryEvidence: Anticipates likely questions from the assessment's purpose and prepares flexible answer outlines rather than memorised scripts
Gives a direct answer first, then a justification and an example, at an appropriate length
Asks for clarification or repetition of a question rather than guessing its meaning
Uses holding phrases to gain thinking time without long silences
Recovers from a word-finding gap or an error by reformulating rather than abandoning the answer
topics.assessmentPrompt: Run a short mock oral on a piece of the learner's own work, including one deliberately ambiguous question and one challenging follow-up. Look for a direct-answer structure, a clarification request in response to the ambiguous question, and reformulation rather than breakdown under the follow-up.

topics.name: Managing test anxiety
topics.description: Recognise how anxiety in evaluative situations (written exams, timed tests, oral assessments and high-stakes proficiency tests) can interfere with performance, particularly through worry that takes up attention, and use preparation, reappraisal and in-exam techniques to reduce its impact, while knowing when anxiety calls for professional support or reasonable adjustments.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the worry (cognitive) and physical or emotional components of their own exam anxiety

Uses at least one technique before the exam (for example, brief writing about worries, or reinterpreting arousal as readiness) and one during it (for example, starting with a question they are confident about, or a planned breathing pause)
Explains how realistic timed practice reduces uncertainty about the exam
Identifies the institutional route to support and adjustments when anxiety is severe
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe what happens to them in the first ten minutes of a high-stakes exam and what they currently do about it. Look for a distinction between thoughts and physical symptoms and at least one specific, plausible technique. Do not attempt to diagnose; the aim is to see whether the learner has a usable repertoire and knows where to get help.

topics.name: University assessment literacy
topics.description: Understand how university assessment works: the difference between formative and summative assessment; how learning outcomes, assessment briefs and marking criteria relate; the range of assessment types; and the rules on weighting, deadlines, word limits, extensions, mitigating circumstances and resits. This knowledge lets learners focus effort where it counts and recognise formative opportunities that carry no marks.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes the formative from the summative tasks in a module and explains how to use each
Traces a stated learning outcome to the assessment task and criteria that measure it
Extracts weighting, deadline, word-limit and submission rules accurately from a module handbook or brief
Explains in general terms the procedures for extensions, mitigating circumstances and resits, and identifies where to check the specific rules
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner an authentic module handbook extract and ask which tasks count towards the final mark and by how much, which learning outcome each task assesses, and what happens if a deadline is missed. Check for accurate extraction and an explanation of why the formative task matters even though it carries no marks.

topics.name: Grading systems
topics.description: Understand how marks are expressed and interpreted in the learner's institution (for example, UK percentage bands and undergraduate degree classifications, master's pass, merit and distinction thresholds, or GPA-style systems) and what grade bands signal about the quality of work, so that marks are neither over- nor under-interpreted against expectations carried over from other systems.
masteryEvidence: Converts a mark into its band or classification under the local scheme and explains what the band indicates about quality
Explains why, in many UK disciplines, marks above about 80% are uncommon and a mark in the 60s can represent good work, contrasting this with systems they know
Identifies the pass mark and the progression or classification rules for their programme
Interprets a mark alongside the written feedback and criteria rather than on its own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Tell the learner they have received 62% for an undergraduate essay at a UK university and ask what this means, how it compares with their previous system, and what information they would need to improve it. Look for correct interpretation (typically the upper second-class band) and recognition that the criteria and feedback, not the number alone, show how to improve.

topics.name: Interpreting marking criteria
topics.description: Unpack the marking criteria, rubrics and grade descriptors for a specific task: identify what each criterion values, how adjacent bands differ, and what evaluative language such as 'critical', 'well-structured' or 'appropriate use of sources' means in observable textual terms, using exemplars to make tacit standards concrete.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites each criterion in a rubric as a concrete question that can be asked of a draft
Identifies the words that distinguish adjacent bands (for example 'some', 'consistent', 'sophisticated') and explains what each would look like in a text
Points to features of an exemplar that justify its band on a given criterion
Ranks two or three exemplars on one criterion and justifies the ranking with textual evidence
Notes which criteria carry most weight and allocates effort accordingly
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner two adjacent bands from a rubric criterion (for example, use of sources) and two short exemplar paragraphs. Ask which band each paragraph fits and why. Look for justifications that cite specific textual features linked to the criterion wording rather than general impressions such as 'it sounds more academic'.

topics.name: Feedback literacy
topics.description: Understand feedback as information that learners must actively make sense of and use, not something simply delivered to them. This involves appreciating its purpose, developing the capacity to make evaluative judgements, managing emotional responses and taking action (Carless and Boud's four features). Feedback is recognised in many forms: written comments, rubric marks, peer comments, discussion in class, tutorials and automated tools.
masteryEvidence: Identifies several sources of feedback in a module, including informal and peer feedback, beyond comments on marked work
Explains what a given comment asks them to do differently
Describes their own emotional response to critical feedback and a strategy for engaging with it constructively
Distinguishes comments directed at the task, the process, self-regulation and the person, and explains which are most useful for future work
Gives an example of feedback they acted on and what resulted
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present five feedback comments of different types (praise of the person, a task-level correction, process advice, a question prompting self-monitoring, a vague comment). Ask the learner to rank them by usefulness and explain. Look for recognition that process-level and self-regulation-level comments carry over to future work, and that praise of the person gives little direction.

topics.name: Acting on feedback
topics.description: Turn feedback into a feed-forward action plan: categorise comments, identify issues that recur across assignments, decide which apply to the next (often different) task, act on them and check whether the change worked.
masteryEvidence: Groups comments from several pieces of work into recurring themes
Distinguishes task-specific comments from those that apply to future assignments
Writes an action plan with specific, checkable actions for each priority comment
Shows in a later draft or task where and how each action was implemented
Uses a short feedback-response note ('In this draft I have tried to…') to direct the marker's attention
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner feedback from two previous assignments and the brief for a new, different task. Ask which comments apply and what they will do differently. Look for transfer of process-level comments (for example, on paragraph focus or source integration) and specific actions, rather than a restatement of the comments.

topics.name: Using written corrective feedback
topics.description: Use written corrective feedback on language (direct corrections, correction codes, underlining or margin indications) to understand the nature of errors, self-correct where feedback is indirect, and track recurring error patterns, recognising that one-off corrections rarely carry over to new writing without follow-up.
masteryEvidence: Interprets a course's correction code and states the rule or pattern behind each coded error
Self-corrects indirectly marked errors and explains the corrections
Distinguishes rule-governed errors (for example subject–verb agreement, articles with countable nouns) from less rule-governed ones (word choice, collocation) and uses different resources for each
Keeps an error log that tallies recurring categories across texts
Edits a new text by checking specifically for their most frequent error categories
topics.assessmentPrompt: Return a paragraph in which five errors are indicated by code but not corrected. Ask the learner to correct each and explain why. Check the accuracy of the corrections and the explanations, and ask whether any of these errors also recur in their other writing.

topics.name: Seeking feedback
topics.description: Request feedback that is specific, timely and usable (on a draft, plan or idea) from tutors, supervisors and peers, framing the request politely and within institutional norms, such as what tutors may comment on before submission, and following up to clarify comments.
masteryEvidence: Writes a feedback request that names the specific aspect to be commented on and why
Checks module or programme rules on pre-submission feedback before asking
Uses suitable mitigation and timing in requests to staff, for example giving sufficient notice and acknowledging workload
Asks follow-up questions that clarify a comment's meaning or request an example of what improvement would look like
Seeks feedback from peers and support services as well as from the assessor
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write a short email to a module tutor requesting feedback on an essay plan. Check that it names specific questions, shows the work done, respects norms and timing, and is appropriately mitigated. 'Please check my essay' with an attachment sent the day before the deadline indicates a gap.

topics.name: Self- and peer-assessment
topics.description: Judge the quality of one's own and peers' work against criteria and exemplars, give feedback that is specific and criterion-referenced, and calibrate these judgements over time by comparing them with tutors' judgements. The aim is evaluative judgement, not self-grading.
masteryEvidence: Rates a draft against criteria and cites textual evidence for each rating
Gives peer comments that identify a specific issue, explain its effect on the reader and suggest a direction, rather than offering generic praise or proofreading
Compares their own judgements with tutor judgements and identifies where and why they diverge
Uses insights from reviewing others' texts to revise their own
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to self-assess a recent draft against two criteria before seeing the tutor's assessment, then compare the two. Look for ratings backed by evidence and, after comparison, an explanation of any divergence (for example, 'I counted my citations; the tutor was looking at how I evaluated them'). Large gaps that the learner cannot explain indicate weak calibration.

topics.name: Metacognitive knowledge
topics.description: Knowledge of oneself as a learner and user of English, of what particular academic tasks demand, and of which strategies suit which tasks and conditions (Flavell's person, task and strategy variables). Accurate metacognitive knowledge allows learners to plan, monitor and adjust their learning rather than relying on habit or on how familiar material feels.
masteryEvidence: Describes their current strengths and gaps across reading, listening, writing and speaking using specific evidence (marks, feedback comments, recurring errors) rather than global labels
Explains how two academic tasks differ in their demands (for example, a source-based coursework essay and a timed short-answer exam) and what that implies for preparation
Names strategies suited to a stated purpose and explains why a familiar strategy such as rereading can create a feeling of knowing without durable learning
Distinguishes a judgement of learning based on familiarity or fluency from one based on a self-test result
Revises a prediction about their own performance after comparing it with the actual outcome
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to predict their score on a short unseen retrieval quiz covering last week's material, take it without notes, then explain any gap between prediction and result and what they would change. Look for explanations framed in terms of task, strategy and self rather than effort or luck alone, and for recognition that familiarity is a weak signal of learning.

topics.name: Self-regulated learning
topics.description: Understand self-regulated learning as a cyclical process of forethought (analysing the task, setting goals, planning strategies, appraising one's self-efficacy), performance (self-monitoring and controlled strategy use) and self-reflection (evaluating outcomes against standards, attributing causes and adapting). The model gives learners and teachers a shared language for locating where independent study breaks down.
masteryEvidence: Describes the three phases of a self-regulation cycle and the main processes in each, using an example from their own study

Analyses a recent assignment or test experience and locates the main breakdown in a specific phase (for example, no analysis of the brief, no monitoring during drafting, no use of feedback afterwards)
Attributes outcomes to controllable factors such as strategy choice and preparation rather than to fixed ability or luck
Proposes a specific adjustment for the next cycle that follows logically from their self-evaluation
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short case of a student who spent many hours on an essay and received a low mark with comments on structure and relevance. Ask the learner what went wrong in each phase and what the student should do next time. Look for phase-specific diagnosis (for example, no analysis of the question or criteria at forethought) and controllable attributions, rather than 'work harder'.

topics.name: Motivation and the L2 self
topics.description: Understand motivation for continued language and academic development through Dörnyei's L2 Motivational Self System (the ideal L2 self, the ought-to L2 self and the learning experience), and use a specific, plausible image of oneself as a competent academic user of English, linked to concrete current actions, to sustain effort beyond an entry requirement or the end of an EAP course.
masteryEvidence: Articulates a specific future academic or professional self that uses English (for example, contributing in lab meetings or writing a dissertation) rather than a generic aim to 'improve my English'
Distinguishes goals they hold for themselves from obligations set by others (entry scores, sponsor or family expectations) and explains how each affects their effort
Links their future-self image to at least two concrete learning actions they are taking now
Identifies features of the current learning experience that support or undermine their motivation and proposes a response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to write three sentences: who they want to be as a user of English in two years, what they must do this month to move towards that, and what will happen if they do nothing. Check specificity, plausibility and the link between vision and action; a vivid image with no linked action, or an action list with no personal purpose, indicates partial understanding.

topics.name: Learner autonomy
topics.description: Understand learner autonomy as a developing capacity to take control over one's learning (choosing objectives, content and methods, and monitoring and evaluating progress) that grows through supported practice, rather than as studying alone or without a teacher. Autonomy underpins the independent study, strategy choice and continued development that universities expect but rarely teach explicitly.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference between autonomy as control over learning decisions and isolation or unsupported self-instruction
Makes and justifies a learning decision that no teacher has prescribed, such as selecting additional materials for a known weakness
Evaluates the outcome of a self-initiated learning activity and decides whether to continue, adapt or abandon it
Identifies constraints on their control in a given context (assessment rules, time, resources) and works within or around them
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask: 'Describe something you learned in English in the last fortnight that no teacher asked you to learn. How did you choose it, how did you go about it, and how did you know whether it worked?' A strong answer shows a self-made decision at each stage; a weak one describes only teacher-set work or an intention without action.

topics.name: Setting language and academic goals
topics.description: Set specific, near-term and checkable language and academic goals derived from actual course and assessment demands, and turn them into planned actions, including if–then plans for predictable obstacles. Well-formed goals turn a general wish to 'improve my English' into decisions about what to practise this week and how progress will be judged.
masteryEvidence: Writes goals that specify the skill or language feature, the context of use, a success indicator and a time frame
Derives goals from evidence (feedback, marking criteria, diagnostic results, programme requirements) rather than general impressions
Breaks a distant goal, such as meeting a progression requirement, into near-term sub-goals with dates
Pairs goals with if–then plans for anticipated obstacles
Reviews and revises goals at planned intervals in the light of progress evidence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner their latest written feedback and ask them to set two goals for the next fortnight. Check whether each goal is traceable to the feedback, specific enough that progress could be checked, and paired with a concrete action and time; 'improve my academic vocabulary' with no action or indicator is a gap response.

topics.name: Time and workload management
topics.description: Plan, prioritise and protect study time across concurrent deadlines: estimating task duration realistically, scheduling backwards from deadlines, allocating time to independent study as well as taught sessions, and recognising and countering procrastination. For L2 learners, realistic estimates must include the extra time that reading and writing in English may take.
masteryEvidence: Produces a weekly plan that includes taught sessions, scheduled independent study blocks and deadlines across modules
Plans backwards from a deadline, breaking a task into dated stages such as reading, planning, drafting and revising, with buffer time
Compares estimated and actual task durations and adjusts future estimates accordingly
Prioritises tasks by deadline, weighting and dependency rather than by preference or ease
Identifies personal procrastination triggers and applies a specific countermeasure
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give the learner a two-week scenario with three overlapping deliverables of different weightings and ask for a schedule. Check for backward planning, prioritisation by weighting and dependency, buffer time and realistic durations; scheduling most work for the final days or ignoring weighting indicates a gap.

topics.name: Independent study
topics.description: Understand the scale and purpose of independent study in higher education systems where expected study hours far exceed contact hours (in many UK institutions one credit conventionally represents about ten notional learning hours), and plan that time productively: preparing for and consolidating taught sessions, following up reading, practising language and progressing assessments without waiting for instructions.
masteryEvidence: Estimates the independent study a module expects from its credit value or handbook and compares this with their current practice
Plans independent study that includes preparation before, and consolidation after, specific taught sessions
Selects independent study activities that address identified needs rather than repeating class activities
Records what independent study was done and its outcome in a form that can be reviewed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner a module handbook page giving credit value and contact hours. Ask how many hours of independent study per week this implies and what they will do in those hours next week. Look for a realistic estimate and activities tied to particular sessions and assessments rather than 'revise' or 'read more'.

topics.name: Evidence-based study techniques
topics.description: Choose and use study techniques that cognitive research rates highly for durable learning (above all retrieval practice and distributed practice, with interleaving and self-explanation as promising options) instead of relying on lower-utility habits such as rereading, highlighting and copying notes. The techniques apply to language items (vocabulary, formulaic phrases, citation conventions) as well as disciplinary content.
masteryEvidence: Converts notes or readings into retrieval questions and self-tests without looking at the source
Schedules several spaced reviews of the same material rather than one massed session
Explains why rereading and highlighting create a sense of familiarity that overestimates learning
Applies retrieval and spacing to language items such as academic collocations and reporting verbs, not only to content
Mixes question or problem types in practice when the assessment will require choosing between methods
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to show how they would prepare for a quiz on a lecture they attended last week, using their own notes. Look for self-testing (cover-and-recall, questions, flashcards) and a spaced schedule; a plan built on rereading and highlighting, or a single long session the night before, indicates a gap.

topics.name: Language learning strategies
topics.description: Select, combine and evaluate strategies for continuing to develop academic English beyond the course: for example, noticing and recording useful language from disciplinary reading, deliberate vocabulary study, seeking opportunities for spoken interaction and feedback, using the L1 as a resource, and managing affect. Strategies are chosen to fit the task and goal rather than out of habit.
masteryEvidence: Names and uses strategies from several categories (memory, cognitive, compensation, metacognitive, affective, social) that fit an identified need
Combines a cluster of strategies for a specific target, such as noticing, recording and retrieving reporting verbs from set readings
Evaluates whether a strategy is working, using evidence, and replaces those that are not
Creates opportunities outside class for language use and feedback (study groups, office hours, extensive reading or listening in the discipline)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to choose one area to improve (for example, following seminar discussion) and to describe the strategies they will use over a month and how they will know whether they are working. Look for a coherent cluster of strategies matched to the target, including monitoring; a list of generic tips ('watch films', 'read more') with no evaluation indicates a gap.

topics.name: Reflective learning logs
topics.description: Keep a structured learning log or journal that records goals, actions taken, evidence of progress and next steps, and use it to make decisions. The key distinction is between analytical reflection, which explains and leads to action, and description of activities or feelings alone.
masteryEvidence: Writes entries that link a learning action to evidence of its effect and a decision about what to do next
Moves beyond description ('Today I read an article') to analysis ('I followed the method section but not the discussion because…')
Reviews earlier entries to identify patterns across weeks and revises goals accordingly
Uses evidence from the log to support a tutorial conversation or an end-of-course reflection
topics.assessmentPrompt: Take three consecutive entries from the learner's log and ask them to summarise what changed in their learning over that period and why. Look for patterns supported by evidence and decisions that follow from them; if the learner cannot draw anything from the entries, the log is functioning as a diary rather than a learning tool.

topics.name: Using academic support services
topics.description: Identify the academic and personal support a university offers (library and subject librarians, writing or academic skills centres, in-sessional EAP, maths and statistics support, disability, wellbeing and advice services) and use it early, with a prepared and specific request, as a normal part of good study practice rather than a last resort.
masteryEvidence: Locates the right service for a given need (statistics help, a reading-list query, a disability adjustment) using institutional web pages or the VLE
Books and prepares for an appointment with a specific question and the relevant materials (draft, brief, feedback)
Distinguishes what a writing or language support service will and will not do, for example advising on a draft but not proofreading it
Seeks support before a deadline becomes a crisis and records what was learned
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three short scenarios (difficulty interpreting statistical output, a lecturer's comment about 'paragraph structure', anxiety that is disrupting sleep before exams) and ask which service the learner would approach, how, and what they would bring. Check for accurate matching, a specific request and awareness of each service's limits.

topics.name: Sustainable study habits and wellbeing
topics.description: Sustain study across a term or degree by anticipating workload peaks, protecting sleep, breaks and social connection, recognising early signs that stress is affecting learning, and knowing when and how to seek help. Wellbeing is treated here as a condition for learning, not as a clinical intervention.
masteryEvidence: Identifies predictable pressure points in their term (assessment clusters, exam season) and plans for them in advance
Maintains routines for sleep and breaks during assessment periods instead of sacrificing them to extend study hours
Recognises personal early-warning signs (avoidance, disrupted sleep, withdrawal from others) and names an action for each
Matches different levels of concern to appropriate institutional or external services, including urgent routes
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to map the next six weeks, marking deadlines and exams, and to note where pressure will peak and what they will do before and during those peaks. Look for anticipation and specific protective actions (earlier starts, reduced commitments, maintained sleep, contact with support) rather than a plan simply to 'work harder'.

topics.name: Learning subject content through English
topics.description: Understand that in foundation, English-medium and degree contexts, disciplinary concepts and the English used to express them are learned together: technical terms, characteristic text types and ways of explaining are part of the content. Learners use this understanding to plan for the double load, for example by previewing terminology, using L1 resources strategically and checking conceptual understanding as well as language.
masteryEvidence: Identifies terms and constructions in a subject text or lecture whose meaning is disciplinary rather than everyday
Distinguishes a comprehension problem caused by the language from one caused by an unfamiliar concept, and applies a different repair to each
Uses L1 or bilingual resources to secure a concept, then re-expresses it in English using the discipline's terms
Explains a disciplinary concept in English at two levels, technical and plain, showing control of both content and language
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short subject-textbook passage containing one sub-technical term (for example 'significant' in a statistics context) and one new concept. Ask the learner to explain the passage, then say which parts were difficult because of the English and which because of the idea. Look for an accurate distinction and a suitable repair strategy for each.

topics.name: Proficiency, achievement and progression assessment
topics.description: Distinguish the purposes of different language assessments (proficiency, placement, diagnostic, achievement, and progression or gatekeeping decisions) and understand that a score is evidence supporting a particular interpretation and decision, not a fixed property of the learner. This helps learners interpret their results realistically and use each assessment for its intended purpose.
masteryEvidence: Classifies assessments they have taken or will take by purpose (an entry test, a placement test, a weekly quiz, a post-entry diagnostic task, a progression assessment)
Explains what decision each assessment informs and who uses the result
Explains why a proficiency test score cannot show what was learned on a particular course, and why a course test cannot certify general proficiency
Recognises that small score differences may fall within measurement error and may not reflect a real difference in ability
topics.assessmentPrompt: Present four assessments (a university's post-entry diagnostic writing task, an international proficiency test, an end-of-unit grammar quiz and a pre-sessional final project). Ask what each is for, who uses the result and for what decision. Look for reasoning about purpose and decision, and for recognition that a diagnostic result is used to guide support, not to decide admission.

topics.name: CEFR levels and entry requirements
topics.description: Understand what CEFR levels describe (communicative ability in can-do terms across activities, including 'plus' levels and uneven profiles across skills), how university and visa entry requirements are expressed through test scores and levels, and why the relationship between a test score and a CEFR level rests on test owners' published alignment claims, which are approximate and debated. Requirements are set by institutions and government bodies and change over time.
masteryEvidence: Explains what a CEFR level describes and why a learner's profile can differ across skills
Reads a programme's entry requirement (overall and minimum component scores) and determines whether a given score profile meets it
Explains that alignments between tests and the CEFR are published by test owners, are approximate, and do not make scores from different tests interchangeable
Distinguishes institutional entry requirements from immigration requirements, using the UK Student route as an example, and identifies the official source for checking current rules
Explains why meeting the entry threshold does not guarantee readiness for all the language demands of a programme
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a programme's entry requirement (an overall score plus minimum component scores) and three score profiles from the same test, one of which meets the overall requirement but misses a component minimum. Ask which profiles meet the requirement and why, and where the learner would check whether it also satisfies current visa rules. Look for attention to component minimums and to current official sources rather than agents or forums.

topics.name: Academic proficiency test formats
topics.description: Understand the task types and constructs of the major academic English proficiency tests used for university entry (for example, reading with selected-response items, lecture-style listening, independent and integrated writing, and interview-based or computer-delivered speaking), including differences in delivery mode and in human, automated or hybrid scoring, so that preparation targets what each test actually measures.
masteryEvidence: Describes the task types in the test they will take and the skills or constructs each targets
Identifies differences in delivery (paper, computer, remote) and scoring (human, automated) that affect preparation
Locates the test's official public assessment criteria for productive tasks and explains each criterion in their own words
Uses official sample materials to work out what tasks require rather than relying on unofficial 'tricks'
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to describe the writing and speaking tasks of the test they intend to take and the criteria used to score them. Look for accurate task descriptions, criterion names explained in their own words, and awareness of delivery and scoring mode; inaccurate or trick-based descriptions indicate reliance on unofficial sources.

topics.name: Test tasks versus university tasks
topics.description: Recognise how proficiency-test tasks differ from university tasks. Test writing is typically short, timed, drawn from personal knowledge or brief inputs, on general topics and scored against generic criteria; university writing is typically extended, source-based, discipline-specific, varied in genre and judged against disciplinary expectations. Learners use this understanding to avoid carrying test templates into university work.
masteryEvidence: Compares a test writing task with a university assignment brief in terms of length, sources, audience, genre, time and criteria
Identifies test-preparation habits (memorised openings, opinion without sources, formulaic linking) that would weaken a university text
Explains why a high test score does not demonstrate control of source-based disciplinary writing
Rewrites a test-style paragraph as a source-based academic paragraph for a specified discipline
topics.assessmentPrompt: Place a test-style opinion essay prompt next to a first-year assignment brief on a similar topic. Ask the learner to list five differences in what each requires and to say which of their test-preparation habits they would need to drop. Look for the difference in source use, differences of genre and audience, and named habits rather than 'university is harder'.

topics.name: Integrated test tasks
topics.description: Handle integrated test tasks that require reading and/or listening before writing or speaking: noting key points from the input efficiently, identifying the relationship between sources (for example, a talk that challenges a reading), selecting and transforming content in one's own words, and organising the response around the task's specific demand within the time limit.
masteryEvidence: Takes notes on the input that capture the main points and the relationships between sources
Selects the source content the task requires rather than summarising everything
Reports source content in their own words with clear attribution to the reading or speaker
Organises the response around the relationship the task specifies, such as how a talk challenges a reading
Completes the response within the time, dividing it between processing the input and producing the response
topics.assessmentPrompt: Use a short reading and a brief talk that challenges it, then ask for a short written response explaining how the talk relates to the reading. Look for the key points from both, an explicit relationship, attribution and transformed wording; copying strings from the reading or omitting the talk indicates a gap.

topics.name: Pre-sessional progression assessment
topics.description: Understand how pre-sessional and similar pathway programmes assess progression, typically through coursework such as an extended source-based essay or report, a small research project, presentations or seminars, portfolios and sometimes timed tasks, and how criteria, weightings, integrity rules and progression thresholds work, so that learners can plan effort across components and use formative stages.
masteryEvidence: Describes each assessed component of their programme, its weighting and the criteria applied
Explains how component results combine into a progression decision, including any minimum per skill
Uses formative stages (outline, draft, tutorial) to improve the summative submission
Explains integrity expectations specific to coursework-based progression, such as rules on drafts, sources, AI tools and proofreading
Contrasts progression assessment with the proficiency test they might otherwise have taken
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to explain, using their programme handbook, how their progression decision will be made and what they would do if draft feedback identified a weakness in source use. Look for an accurate account of components, weightings and thresholds, and a plan that uses formative feedback and support rather than waiting for the final mark.

dependencies.reason: Exams are one category of summative assessment; understanding assessment types and rules frames the differences between exam formats
Analysing an exam question depends on knowing what each command word demands
Unpacking coursework briefs is usually taught first; exam question analysis applies the same procedure at speed
Time allocation and expected answer types depend on the paper's format and mark scheme
A revision plan is only effective if its sessions use retrieval and spacing rather than rereading
Spacing revision across weeks and modules requires backward planning from the exam timetable
What to revise and how depends on whether the exam is seen, unseen, objective or open-book
Revision draws on notes that have been reworked into material suitable for self-testing
Writing under time pressure is only effective if the question has first been correctly interpreted and time allocated
Timed writing compresses outlining into a few minutes, which presupposes the ability to plan a structure from a position
Producing text fluently without stopping to edit is a drafting habit that timed conditions demand
Strategy depends on the paper's item types and scoring rules, such as negative marking
Stems often contain dense noun phrases, negatives and embedded clauses that must be parsed accurately
Distinguishing correct from incorrect options often depends on qualifiers and absolutes (tend to, in most cases, always)
Open-book preparation depends on knowing what the format permits and what it rewards
Usable open-book materials are notes that record sources and separate quotation, paraphrase and own comment
Take-home exams require a clear understanding of the boundary between permitted collaboration and collusion
Oral examination is largely sustained question handling: clarifying, answering, and responding to challenge
Preparation depends on the type of oral assessment and what it is designed to test
Recovering from breakdowns under examination pressure relies on self-repair and reformulation
Managing exam anxiety builds on general routines for stress, sleep and help-seeking
Familiarity with the format reduces uncertainty, one source of anticipatory worry
Handbooks and briefs use terms such as module, credit, learning outcome, extension and extenuating circumstances that must be understood first
Knowing that university study expects independence and criticality explains why assessment rewards these qualities
Grade conventions are expressed through institutional vocabulary (classification, pass mark, resit, merit) that learners need first
Criteria only make sense in relation to the learning outcomes and assessment tasks they operationalise
Rubrics are organised by grade bands, so learners need to know what each band signifies
Criteria use the same evaluative verbs and nouns as assignment questions (analyse, evaluate, critical), whose demands must be known
Appreciating feedback presupposes understanding the formative purpose of assessment
Feedback is useful as information within the self-regulation cycle; learners need that frame to see feedback as something to act on
Planning action on feedback requires first understanding comments as information to use and managing the emotional response to them
Mapping comments to criteria shows which comments carry most weight and how they apply to other tasks
A feed-forward plan is a set of specific, checkable goals derived from evidence
Engaging with language corrections rather than copying them depends on viewing feedback as information to act on
Correction codes rely on grammatical metalanguage (subject, verb, clause) that learners need in order to interpret and apply them
Asking for targeted feedback requires knowing what kinds of feedback are useful and how they will be used
Feedback requests to staff are requests with high imposition and need appropriate mitigation and framing
Judging quality against criteria requires first being able to interpret what the criteria and bands mean
Making evaluative judgements is one of the components of feedback literacy, and peer review also involves giving feedback in usable form
Planning, monitoring and evaluating learning presuppose knowledge of one's own abilities, of task demands and of the strategies available
The forethought phase includes self-motivation beliefs (self-efficacy, valuing of the outcome), which motivational self-images help sustain
Taking control of learning decisions depends on knowing which strategies and resources suit which tasks and one's own needs
Goal setting is a forethought process whose value lies in providing the standard for later self-monitoring and self-evaluation
Academic goals must be derived from what university study actually requires (independence, criticality, participation)
Prioritising and scheduling require explicit goals and sub-goals to allocate time against
Productive independent study depends on scheduling and protecting non-contact hours
Independent study requires learners to choose what to study and how, without teacher direction
Independent study hours are only productive if filled with effective techniques such as self-testing rather than rereading
Choosing retrieval and spacing over rereading requires strategy knowledge and awareness that familiarity misleads judgements of learning
Orchestrating and evaluating strategies is self-regulation applied to language development: planning, monitoring and adapting strategy use
Retrieval and spacing are the memory mechanisms behind effective deliberate study of vocabulary and phraseology
Continuing language development beyond the course depends on learners taking control of what and how they practise
Log entries are evaluated against goals; without goals, entries become description with no standard for judging progress
Using a log to make decisions presupposes that the learner, not only the teacher, makes learning decisions
Finding the right service depends on understanding how the institution's schools, central services and roles are organised
Deciding when to seek help is a monitoring and adaptation decision within the self-regulation cycle
Anticipating workload peaks and protecting rest depend on planning study time across the term
Knowing which wellbeing, advice and disability services exist is needed to act on early-warning signs
Distinguishing language problems from concept problems depends on understanding how background knowledge supports comprehension
Understanding lexical coverage explains why unknown technical and sub-technical words can block comprehension of subject texts
Managing the double load relies on deliberate strategies for noticing, recording and using disciplinary language
Entry requirements are a gatekeeping use of proficiency scores; interpreting them requires understanding assessment purposes and score interpretation
Test formats are designed for the proficiency purpose; knowing that purpose explains why tasks are general rather than course-based
Comparing test tasks with university tasks requires accurate knowledge of what the test tasks are
The comparison depends on knowing the range of genres students are assessed on at university
The central difference is the role of sources in university writing, which learners need to understand to see what test writing lacks
Strategies for integrated tasks depend on knowing the specific task structure and constraints of the test
Integrated test tasks apply the general reading/listening-to-writing skills of selecting and transforming source content under test conditions
Integrated test responses are produced under strict time limits and draw on rapid planning and time allocation
Progression decisions are made against published criteria, which learners must interpret to plan and self-assess
Progression outcomes are usually expressed as equivalents to entry requirements, so learners need to understand how those are framed
Coursework-based progression is designed to be closer to university tasks than tests are; understanding the difference explains its design

guidance.summary: Bachman and Palmer (2010) show that the characteristics of an assessment task shape what it measures, and this applies to university exam formats as much as to language tests: a seen essay paper, an open-book problem paper and a multiple-choice test reward different preparation. Horowitz (1986), analysing writing tasks and exam questions set by university staff, found that they mostly required students to select and reorganise material for a specified purpose rather than to express personal opinion. Teach formats through the learner's own past papers and regulations, and draw out what each format rewards.

activities.title: Past paper anatomy
learnerActions: Find a past paper for one of your modules
Note the format, number of questions, choice, marks per question and permitted materials
Identify what each question type asks you to do (recall, explain, apply, evaluate)
Write a one-paragraph preparation brief for this paper
activities.intendedInsight: Each exam has a design that tells you what kind of preparation will pay off.
activities.rationale: Task characteristics determine what an assessment measures (Bachman & Palmer, 2010); reading a paper's design is the first step in preparing for it.

activities.title: Format-to-preparation matching
learnerActions: Match six exam formats to the preparation each needs
Discuss formats you have not met before
Identify which of your own exams use which format
activities.intendedInsight: Preparation that works for one format may be wasted effort for another.
activities.rationale: Making differences between formats explicit helps learners from systems dominated by a single exam type.

difficulties.pattern: Assuming all exams test memory of lecture content.
difficulties.revealedBy: Revision that consists only of memorising notes, even for application or open-book papers.
difficulties.response: Show past questions that require application or evaluation and discuss what memorised content alone would produce.

difficulties.pattern: 'Open-book means easy.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Little preparation for open-book papers; time spent searching notes during the exam.
difficulties.response: Show the higher-order demands of open-book questions and the time cost of unorganised materials.

difficulties.pattern: Unfamiliarity with negative marking, online invigilation or computer-based exam rules.
difficulties.revealedBy: Questions about rules on the day; procedural errors.
difficulties.response: Point learners to the exam regulations and, where possible, provide a practice session in the actual system.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'What format is your next exam, and how will that change the way you prepare?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the format accurately and names preparation specific to it.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Knows the format but describes generic preparation.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not know the format.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners often meet several unfamiliar formats in their first year of subject modules. Pre-sessional learners meet mainly timed writing and oral assessment. In-sessional UG and PGT learners need this before each exam season, particularly where formats (such as take-home or case-based exams) are new to them.
reviewNotes: Exam formats, especially online and take-home variants, change frequently and vary across institutions.

guidance.summary: Under time pressure, writers may fall back on what Bereiter and Scardamalia (1987) call knowledge telling, retrieving content on the topic without transforming it to address the rhetorical problem. In an exam this produces answers that 'write all I know' instead of answering the question. Horowitz (1986) found that university tasks typically ask students to select and organise material for a specific purpose. Teach a fast, routine analysis of command, topic, focus and limiting words, and practise distinguishing questions on the same topic that require different answers.

activities.title: Same topic, different question
learnerActions: Read three questions on the same topic with different command and limiting words
For each, mark the command, topic, focus and limiting words
Write a one-sentence description of what a good answer would do
Compare with a partner and discuss how the three answers would differ
activities.intendedInsight: The same topic can require very different answers, and the question's wording decides which.
activities.rationale: Contrasting questions makes visible the transformation demand that knowledge telling misses (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987).

activities.title: Marks-to-minutes calculation
learnerActions: Take a past paper and calculate the time available per mark
Allocate minutes to each question, including planning and checking time
Compare your allocation with how you actually spent your time in a previous exam
activities.intendedInsight: Time should follow marks, and planning time is part of the allocation.
activities.rationale: Proportional time allocation prevents over-investment in early questions, a common performance problem in timed exams.

difficulties.pattern: Recognising a revised topic in the question and writing a prepared answer that does not address the specific question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that are relevant to the topic but not to the question; feedback such as 'does not answer the question'.
difficulties.response: Practise with questions that deliberately twist familiar topics. Where learners come from assessment systems that rewarded reproducing model answers, make the different expectation explicit rather than criticising the habit.

difficulties.pattern: Misreading limiting words (dates, contexts, 'with reference to') under pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Answers that go outside the specified scope.
difficulties.response: Build a habit of marking limiting words before planning. Do not respond by adding more content to revise; the problem is reading, not knowledge.

difficulties.pattern: Spending too long on the first question and running out of time.
difficulties.revealedBy: Unfinished final answers; very long first answers.
difficulties.response: Practise timed papers with fixed time checkpoints.

diagnostic.task: Give one exam question and ask the learner to explain, in one sentence, what a good answer must do.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies the command, focus and limits and describes the required answer shape, including any judgement required.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Identifies the topic and command word but misses limiting words or implicit sub-questions.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Restates the topic only.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and in-sessional UG learners need this for subject exams. Pre-sessional learners apply it to timed tasks in progression assessment. PGT learners face questions that often require critical evaluation within tightly specified contexts.

guidance.summary: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated practice testing and distributed practice as the most useful learning techniques, and Cepeda et al. (2006) found that the best spacing between study sessions grows with the delay before the test. Roediger and Karpicke (2006) found that retrieval practice beat restudy on delayed tests. Revision planning applies these findings: start early, revisit topics several times, build sessions around retrieval and past questions, and adjust the plan using self-test results.

activities.title: Topic-by-week spaced grid
learnerActions: List all topics for the exam
Build a grid of weeks before the exam and schedule each topic at least three times, with growing gaps
Assign a retrieval activity to each session (blank-page recall, past question, self-test)
Update the grid weekly according to your self-test results
activities.intendedInsight: Revisiting topics several times with retrieval works better than covering each topic once.
activities.rationale: The grid operationalises distributed practice and practice testing (Dunlosky et al., 2013; Cepeda et al., 2006).

activities.title: Blank-page recall plus past question
learnerActions: Write everything you can remember about a topic on a blank page without notes
Check against your notes and mark gaps in a different colour
Attempt a past question on the topic under time pressure
Record the gaps for your next session on this topic
activities.intendedInsight: Gaps you discover through recall are what to study next.
activities.rationale: Retrieval both strengthens memory and reveals what is not yet known (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006).

difficulties.pattern: Cramming in the final days.
difficulties.revealedBy: Revision plans that start a few days before the exam; late nights.
difficulties.response: Help learners plan backwards from exam dates early in the term. Do not simply warn against cramming; show the delayed-test evidence and give a concrete plan.

difficulties.pattern: Revising favourite topics repeatedly and avoiding difficult ones.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uneven self-test results that do not change the plan.
difficulties.response: Require a weekly reallocation based on self-test results.

difficulties.pattern: Revision means making beautiful summary notes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Large amounts of time spent rewriting notes; little self-testing.
difficulties.response: Turn summary-making into a retrieval activity: summarise from memory, then check.

diagnostic.task: Ask: 'When will you start revising for your next exam, and what will a typical session look like?'
diagnostic.strongResponse: Starts weeks ahead, revisits topics, uses retrieval and past papers, and adjusts according to results.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Starts early but plans to reread, or uses retrieval but only in the final days.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Plans to start in the final week by reading notes.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners preparing for their first subject exams need explicit planning support. In-sessional UG and PGT learners benefit from short sessions before exam seasons, ideally with subject past papers. Pre-sessional courses rarely include content exams, so the topic is not listed there.

guidance.summary: Ellis and Yuan (2004) found that pre-task planning increased the fluency and syntactic complexity of L2 writing, while unpressured on-line planning favoured accuracy, which suggests a trade-off that timed conditions make acute. Weigle (2002) discusses timed impromptu writing as an assessment format, including its limitations as a measure of academic writing. Under time pressure writers may revert to knowledge telling (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987). Teach a short, routine planning phase, disciplined time allocation and targeted final checking, and present timed writing as a distinct performance rather than a compressed version of coursework writing.

activities.title: Short plan drill
learnerActions: Read an unseen question and give yourself a few minutes only to write a position and three to four points
Write the answer within the remaining time
Compare your plan with the finished script: did you follow it?
Repeat weekly with new questions and track whether your plans become quicker and more usable
activities.intendedInsight: A brief plan keeps a timed answer focused and does not waste time.
activities.rationale: Ellis and Yuan (2004) found benefits of pre-task planning for fluency and complexity; the drill makes short planning automatic.

activities.title: Graduated time compression
learnerActions: Write an answer with generous time
Write an answer to a similar question with less time, then with exam-length time
Compare the three scripts and note what was lost (accuracy, development, conclusion)
Decide what to protect under pressure and plan your checking routine accordingly
activities.intendedInsight: Knowing what slips under time pressure lets you decide in advance what to protect.
activities.rationale: Weigle (2002) notes that timed writing captures a particular kind of performance; experiencing the effect of time limits helps learners manage it deliberately.

difficulties.pattern: 'There's no time to plan.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Scripts that wander, change position midway or stop without a conclusion.
difficulties.response: Show planned and unplanned scripts side by side. Do not demand elaborate plans: a position and a few points are enough.

difficulties.pattern: Reproducing a memorised essay that does not fit the question.
difficulties.revealedBy: Fluent, accurate scripts that are off-question; identical openings across scripts.
difficulties.response: Use questions that require adapting known content, and give feedback specifically on relevance.

difficulties.pattern: Accuracy declines sharply under time pressure.
difficulties.revealedBy: More errors in timed scripts than in coursework from the same learner.
difficulties.response: Teach a short final check for the learner's most frequent error types. Do not expect error-free timed writing or penalise it as though it were edited coursework.

diagnostic.task: Set a short timed question and look at the plan and script together.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A brief plan with a position, followed by a script that answers the question directly, develops the planned points and finishes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A plan exists but is abandoned, or the script is relevant but unfinished.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No plan; a script that drifts or does not address the question.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and in-sessional UG learners use this for subject exam essays and short answers. Pre-sessional learners use it in timed progression tasks and test preparation. PGT learners meet timed writing less often, but it matters where modules use exams.
reviewNotes: Ellis and Yuan's study used narrative writing with planning-time manipulations; extending its findings to argumentative exam essays is an inference.

guidance.summary: Practice testing, including with objective formats, is itself a high-utility learning technique (Dunlosky et al., 2013), so preparation and test performance reinforce each other. Item-writing guidance advises against negatively worded stems and absolute terms (Haladyna et al., 2002), which suggests that well-constructed university items may be less vulnerable to cue-based 'test-wise' strategies than learners believe. For L2 readers the main difficulties are often linguistic (negatives, qualifiers, dense stems), so emphasise precise reading and knowledge over tricks.

activities.title: Qualifier spotting
learnerActions: Read a set of stems and options and underline every negative, absolute and qualifier
Rephrase each stem in plain English
Explain how each underlined word changes which option is correct
activities.intendedInsight: Small words such as 'not', 'always' and 'usually' can decide the answer.
activities.rationale: Qualifiers and negatives are a known source of misreading, and item-writing guidance treats them as potential problems (Haladyna et al., 2002).

activities.title: Cover the options
learnerActions: Cover the options and answer the stem from knowledge
Uncover the options and look for your answer
If it is not there, eliminate options with stated reasons
Review which items you could answer before seeing options
activities.intendedInsight: Answering from knowledge first reduces the pull of plausible-looking distractors.
activities.rationale: Generating an answer before reading options is a form of retrieval practice (Dunlosky et al., 2013) and reduces reliance on recognising familiar wording.

difficulties.pattern: Missing 'NOT' or 'EXCEPT' in a stem.
difficulties.revealedBy: Choosing a true statement when asked for the false one.
difficulties.response: Train a habit of marking negatives before reading options.

difficulties.pattern: Choosing the option whose wording is most familiar from lectures.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors on application items where a distractor reuses lecture phrasing.
difficulties.response: Practise items where the correct answer is paraphrased and the distractor uses familiar wording.

difficulties.pattern: Relying on cue-based tricks such as 'choose the longest answer'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Learners report rules of thumb in place of reasoning.
difficulties.response: Show that well-written items avoid such cues and redirect effort to knowledge and precise reading.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to answer one 'NOT' item and one qualifier item aloud.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Notices the negative and qualifier, reasons about each option and selects correctly.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Selects correctly but cannot explain, or notices the negative only when prompted.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misses the negative or qualifier.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners often meet objective tests in science, business and health modules. In-sessional UG and PGT learners meet them in quantitative and professional programmes. Pre-sessional courses rarely use subject objective tests, although proficiency tests use selected-response formats.
reviewNotes: No bibliography source directly addresses L2 learners' performance on content multiple-choice items; haladyna2002 is proposed and concerns item writing rather than test taking.

guidance.summary: Open-book and take-home exams shift the demand from recall to application, analysis and synthesis, and increase the importance of organised materials and integrity awareness. The Handbook of Academic Integrity (Bretag, 2016) covers the forms of misconduct, including collusion and contract cheating, that unsupervised formats can make more tempting. Pecorari (2013) emphasises teaching good source use rather than only policing it. Teach learners to prepare indexed materials, to write answers that apply rather than transcribe, and to check paper-specific rules, especially on collaboration and AI use, which vary and change.

activities.title: Index your resources
learnerActions: Organise your notes for one module into a structure with tabs or a contents page
Create a one-page index of key concepts, cases or formulae with locations
Test it by finding five items against a timer
Revise the index where retrieval was slow
activities.intendedInsight: In open-book exams, the speed of finding information depends on preparation done beforehand.
activities.rationale: Time spent searching unorganised materials reduces time for analysis, which is what these formats reward.

activities.title: Reproduction versus application
learnerActions: Compare two answers to a take-home question: one assembled from notes and one that applies concepts to the question
Identify which parts of each answer the question actually asked for
Rewrite a paragraph of the first answer so that it applies rather than reproduces
activities.intendedInsight: Having access to notes does not mean copying them; the marks are for using them.
activities.rationale: Pecorari (2013) argues for teaching purposeful source use; open-book answers are a case in which source material must be transformed to serve a new purpose.

difficulties.pattern: 'Open-book is easier, so I'll revise less.'
difficulties.revealedBy: Little preparation; answers that reproduce notes.
difficulties.response: Show the higher-order demands of open-book questions and the time cost of searching.

difficulties.pattern: Copying from notes, slides or sources without attribution under time pressure.
